displayQuote: God is where you let Him in

meta.title: Who really said "God is where you let Him in"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: No — Paulo Coelho didn't coin it. "God is where you let Him in" is a famous Hasidic saying of the Kotzker Rebbe (1787–1859), recorded by Buber and Kaplan.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'God is where you let Him in'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Paulo Coelho. It's a 19th-century Hasidic teaching of the Kotzker Rebbe — 'God dwells wherever man lets him in.'

answer.label: Not Paulo Coelho — a Hasidic saying of the Kotzker Rebbe
answer.authorName: Menachem Mendel of Kotzk (the Kotzker Rebbe)
answer.authorDates: 1787–1859 · Hasidic rabbi & Torah master of Kotzk
answer.sourceLine: This is a paraphrase of a famous Hasidic teaching, not a line from Paulo Coelho. Asked “Where does God dwell?” the Kotzker Rebbe answered, “Wherever you let Him in” — recorded by Martin Buber and, in the exact “let Him in” wording, by Aryeh Kaplan. No Coelho book is a documented source for it.

source.heading: Where the line really comes from

docMeta.dd: Hasidic saying of the Kotzker Rebbe
The Way of Man According to the Teaching of Hasidism
Martin Buber (retelling); wording “let Him in” per Aryeh Kaplan

source.excerpt: “Where is the dwelling of God?” With this question the Rabbi of Kotzk surprised a number of learned men who happened to be visiting him. They laughed at him: “What a thing to ask! Is not the whole world full of his glory?” Then he answered his own question: “God dwells wherever man lets him in.”
trail: Wikiquote lists the line in its Misattributed section for Paulo Coelho, tracing it to the Kotzker Rebbe as quoted in Aryeh Kaplan’s Innerspace (1990), p. 160.
Martin Buber records the classic form — “God dwells wherever man lets him in” — in The Way of Man According to the Teaching of Hasidism.

The attribution to the Kotzker Rebbe is echoed independently, e.g. this Reconstructionist d’var Torah: “the Kotzker Rebbe was once asked: ‘Where does God dwell?’ to which he replied, ‘Wherever you let Him in.’”
source.excerptNote: Martin Buber’s retelling of the Kotzker teaching. Aryeh Kaplan gives a childhood version in which the young Rebbe says “God is only where you let Him in” — the popular Coelho meme simply drops the “only.”
source.rightsNote: The teaching is a 19th-century oral Hasidic saying, but the exact English wording “God is where you let Him in” is a modern rendering that cannot be tied to any specific pre-1931 publication. The earliest documented English forms are themselves in copyright — Martin Buber’s The Way of Man (English, 1950) and Aryeh Kaplan’s Innerspace (1990) — so no public-domain status can be asserted for this precise phrasing.

author.name: Menachem Mendel of Kotzk
author.heading: About Menachem Mendel of Kotzk
author.metaLine: 1787–1859 · Hasidic rabbi & Torah master of Kotzk, Poland
author.bio: Menachem Mendel Morgensztern of Kotzk was a fiercely demanding Hasidic master known for his uncompromising pursuit of inner truth and terse, piercing aphorisms. The teaching that God is present wherever a person admits Him is among the sayings most tied to his name, transmitted through Hasidic tradition and popularized in the West by Martin Buber.

misattribution.heading: Why Coelho gets the credit
misattribution.intro: Like most feel-good spiritual one-liners, this drifts to a famous modern name. But its real home is Hasidic Judaism, not Paulo Coelho’s fiction.

items.scope: “God is where you let Him in”
items.why: Widely circulated on quote sites and social media as Coelho’s, but it appears in none of his books as a sourced line; Wikiquote files it under Misattributed and points to the Kotzker Rebbe.

items.who: The Kotzker Rebbe (Menachem Mendel of Kotzk)
items.why: The saying answers the question “Where does God dwell?” with “Wherever you let Him in” — recorded by Martin Buber and, in the “let Him in” wording, by Aryeh Kaplan’s Innerspace.

misattribution.truthLine: The thought is genuinely old and genuinely Jewish — a Kotzker Hasidic teaching preserved by Buber and later teachers — and the popular “Paulo Coelho” credit is simply wrong.

context.heading: A teaching about presence, not geography
lead: The Kotzker Rebbe’s point cuts against easy piety. The visitors assume the answer is obvious — the whole world is full of God’s glory. His reply reframes the question: divine presence is not a fact of geography but a matter of consent. God dwells wherever a person actually lets Him in.

In Buber’s hands the story becomes a parable about authentic living: we can admit God only “where we really stand, where we live a true life.” That is a long way from a decorative Instagram caption — and a long way from Paulo Coelho.
detailsBody: Buber’s form: “God dwells wherever man lets him in” — from The Way of Man According to the Teaching of Hasidism.
Kaplan’s childhood version: the five-year-old Rebbe tells his father, “God is only where you let Him in” — Innerspace (1990), p. 160. The popular Coelho meme drops “only” and swaps in “is where.”
